From the alternatives given below, choose the correct meaning of the idiom
'a flash in the pan'.

options.text: To abruptly turn on, as of lights
Someone or something whose success or popularity is short-lived
To look at one, usually quickly and perhaps unexpectedly
To be thought of in a quick or fleeting fashion

questions.solution: The correct answer is: **Someone or something whose success or popularity is short-lived**. **__Key Points__** __ • The idiom **'a flash in the pan'** refers to something that starts out with great **promise** but soon fails or is not repeated; it implies a **temporary** success. (क्षणभंगुर सफलता) • **Example: **The new company's high profits last month proved to be just **a flash in the pan** when they went bankrupt this month. • **'Someone or something whose success or popularity is short-lived'** describes a person or thing that achieves **fame** or success for a very brief period and then disappears from the spotlight. (अल्पकालिक सफलता) • **Example: **Many pop stars of the 90s were just **short-lived** sensations who are no longer remembered today. • Hence, we can infer that the meaning of the idiom **'a flash in the pan'** is **'someone or something whose success or popularity is short-lived'**. Therefore, the correct answer is: **Someone or something whose success or popularity is short-lived**. **Additional Information__** Here are the other options explained along with their Hindi meanings and example sentences: • **To abruptly turn on** (अचानक चालू होना): To start or activate something, especially **lights** or **machinery**, very suddenly. • **Example:** The security lights **abruptly turned on** as soon as the thief climbed over the wall. • **To look at one** (एक नज़र देखना): To cast a quick or **unexpected** glance at someone or something. • **Example: **She took a **quick look at** him to see if he was joking. • **To be thought of in a quick or fleeting fashion** (क्षणभर के लिए विचार में आना): When an **idea** or thought passes through the mind very **rapidly** without staying. • **Example:** For a second, the idea of quitting his job was **thought of in a fleeting fashion**, but he decided to stay. 31:Ta8c, The correct answer is: **Enlarge**.

questions.question: Which of the following words is the closest synonym of the word "expand"?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **Enlarge**.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The word **'expand'** means to increase in **size**, **volume**, or **quantity**, or to make something become **larger**. (विस्तार करना)
 
 
• **Example:** Metals tend to **expand** when they are heated.
 
 
 
• **'Enlarge'** means to make something **bigger** or to become **larger** in size or scale. It is the closest synonym for 'expand' as both describe the process of increasing dimensions. (बड़ा करना)
 
 
• **Example:** We are planning to **enlarge** our kitchen to make more space for dining.
 
 
 
• Hence, we can infer that the synonym of **'expand'** is **'enlarge'**.

Therefore, the correct answer is- **Enlarge**.

**Additional Information__**

Here are the other options explained along with their Hindi meanings and example sentences:

 
• **Reduce **(कम करना): To make something **smaller** or **less** in amount, degree, or size.
 
 
• **Example:** You need to **reduce** the speed of the car as you approach the intersection.
 
 
 
• **Hide **(छिपाना): To put or keep something out of **sight** or to keep a secret.
 
 
• **Example:** He tried to **hide** the broken vase behind the curtain.
 
 
 
• **Destroy **(नष्ट करना): To end the **existence** of something by damaging it so badly that it cannot be repaired.
 
 
• **Example:** The heavy **earthquake** managed to **destroy** many old buildings in the city.

Therefore, the correct answer is- **Acumen**. **Additional Information__** Here are the other options explained along with their Hindi meanings and example sentences: __ • **Contrition** (पछतावा/अनुताप): The state of feeling remorseful and penitent for a sin or shortcoming. • **Example:** The defendant showed genuine **contrition** for his actions during the trial. • **Candor** (स्पष्टवादिता/निष्कपटता): The quality of being open and honest in expression; frankness. • **Example:** We were surprised by the **candor** of her confession regarding the mistake. • **Abnegation** (त्याग/अस्वीकार): The act of renouncing or rejecting something, typically a right, belief, or pleasure. • **Example:** Her life was marked by self-sacrifice and the **abnegation** of material comforts. 37:Te32, The correct answer is **Classical music is played by the orchestra at the concert hall every weekend**__.

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?
The orchestra plays classical music at the concert hall every weekend.

options.text: Classical music is played by the orchestra at the concert hall every weekend.
Classical music was played by the orchestra at the concert hall every weekend.
Classical music has been played by the orchestra at the concert hall every weekend.
Classical music is being played by the orchestra at the concert hall every weekend.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Classical music is played by the orchestra at the concert hall every weekend**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The provided sentence is in the **Simple Present Tense**, which is used to describe habitual actions, general truths, or routines. This is identified by the base verb **plays** (V1+s) following the singular subject **The orchestra**.
 
• In the **Active Voice**, the structure follows the pattern: **Subject + Verb (s/es) + Object**. In this instance, **The orchestra** is the subject performing the action, and **classical music** is the direct object receiving the action.
 
• To convert a sentence from **Active to Passive Voice** in the **Simple Present Tense**, the object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive sentence. The grammatical formula is: **New Subject + is/am/are + Past Participle (V3) + by + Agent (Optional)**.
 
• The term **Classical music** is an uncountable noun and is treated as **singular**. Therefore, the auxiliary verb **is** must be used to maintain **Subject-Verb Agreement**.
 
• The **Past Participle** form of the verb **play** is **played**. Consequently, the core passive structure becomes **is played**.
 
• The **agent** of the action, **the orchestra**, is introduced using the preposition **by**. The phrase **at the concert hall every weekend** serves as an **Adverbial of Place and Time** and remains at the end of the sentence to preserve the original context and frequency.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• Analysis of incorrect tense conversions:
 
 
• **Simple Past Passive**: The phrase **was played** is used only if the original sentence was in the **Simple Past** (e.g., 'The orchestra played'). Since the original action is habitual/present, this is incorrect.
 
• **Present Continuous Passive**: The structure **is being played** is reserved for actions currently in progress at the time of speaking. It does not fit the **every weekend** habitual context.
 
• **Present Perfect Passive**: The construction **has been played** indicates an action that started in the past and has just been completed or continues to have relevance, which changes the **Simple Present** meaning.
 
 
 
• **Transitive Verbs**: Only sentences with **transitive verbs** (verbs that take an object) can be converted into the passive voice. Here, **plays** is transitive as it acts upon **classical music**.
</ul

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?
Are you preparing a science quiz for the children?

options.text: Was a science quiz being prepared by you for the children?
Are a science quiz being prepared by you for the children?
Has a science quiz being prepared by you for the children?
Is a science quiz being prepared by you for the children?

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Is a science quiz being prepared by you for the children?**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The given sentence is an **interrogative sentence** written in the **Present Continuous Tense**. The active voice structure is: **Am/Is/Are + Subject + V1 + ing + Object?**.

• To convert a **Present Continuous** sentence into **Passive Voice**, the structure used is: **Am/Is/Are + New Subject + being + Past Participle (V3) + by + New Object?**.

• In the active sentence, the **subject** is **you** and the **object** is **a science quiz**. During conversion, **a science quiz** becomes the **new subject** of the passive sentence.

• Since the new subject **a science quiz** is **singular**, the helping verb **Is** must be placed at the beginning of the sentence to maintain the **interrogative form**.

• The main verb **preparing** is changed into its **Past Participle** form, which is **prepared**. The auxiliary word **being** is added before the past participle to indicate the **continuous aspect** of the action in the passive state.

• The original subject **you** becomes the **agent** of the action, introduced by the preposition **by**. The phrase **for the children** remains as an additional adjunct at the end of the clause.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Incorrect Tense and Subject-Verb Agreement**:

• **Was a science quiz...**: This option is incorrect because it uses the **Past Continuous Tense** auxiliary verb **Was**, which changes the timeframe of the original **Present Continuous** sentence.

• **Are a science quiz...**: This option is grammatically incorrect because it fails to follow **Subject-Verb Agreement**. The plural verb **Are** cannot be used with the singular subject **a science quiz**.

• **Has a science quiz...**: This option incorrectly utilizes the **Present Perfect Tense** helping verb. The **Present Perfect Passive** requires the structure **Has/Have + Subject + been + V3**, which does not match the continuous nature of the original question.

</ul

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?
The gates were being painted by the workers all afternoon.

options.text: The workers painted the gates all afternoon.
The workers had painted the gates all afternoon.
The workers were painting the gates all afternoon.
The workers will paint the gates all afternoon.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The workers were painting the gates all afternoon.**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The given sentence is in the **Passive Voice** and follows the **Past Continuous Tense** structure. The passive form for this tense is: **Subject + was/were + being + Past Participle (V3) + by + Agent**.

• To convert the sentence into the **Active Voice**, the **Agent** (the workers) must be shifted to the **Subject** position, and the **Passive Subject** (the gates) must be shifted to the **Object** position.

• The auxiliary verb **being** is removed, and the **Past Participle** (painted) is changed back into its **Present Participle** form (painting) to reflect continuous action in the past.

• The active structure for the **Past Continuous Tense** is: **Subject + was/were + Present Participle (V-ing) + Object**. Since **The workers** is a plural noun, the auxiliary verb **were** is retained.

• Combining these elements, the sentence becomes 'The workers were painting the gates all afternoon'.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Tense Variations**:

• **Simple Past Tense**: Used for actions completed at a specific time in the past. The active form is 'The workers **painted** the gates'.

• **Past Perfect Tense**: Used to describe an action that was completed before another action or time in the past. The active form is 'The workers **had painted** the gates'.

• **Simple Future Tense**: Used for actions that will happen after the current moment. The active form is 'The workers **will paint** the gates'.

• **Active vs. Passive Voice**:

• In **Active Voice**, the subject performs the action. It is more direct and emphasizes the **doer**.

• In **Passive Voice**, the subject receives the action. It is often used when the **action** itself or the **receiver** is more important than the doer.

</ul

questions.question:
Select the correct alternative to fill in the blank with the correct preposition in the following sentence.

The French are very proud ______ their valour.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**of**'. **__Key Points__** __ 
• The adjective **proud** is habitually followed by the preposition **of** when referring to the object of one's pride. 
• The phrase **proud of** means feeling deep pleasure or satisfaction as a result of one's own achievements, qualities, or possessions. 
• In this context, the sentence indicates that the **French** feel a sense of pride regarding their **valour** (great courage in the face of danger). 
• Using any other preposition like **in**, **at**, or **about** with the adjective **proud** is grammatically incorrect. Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 1**. **Complete Sentence:** *'The French are very **proud of**__ their valour.'* **__Additional Information__** 
• **Take pride in:** While we use the preposition **of** with the adjective **proud**, we use the preposition **in** with the noun **pride** (e.g., They **take pride in** their work). 
• **Option 2: 'in'** is used with the verb/noun form (**pride in**) but not with the adjective **proud**. 
• **Option 3: 'at'** and **Option 4: 'about'** are not standard collocations for expressing pride in English grammar. </ul

questions.question:
A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option which can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. In case Options A, B and C are not found suitable, choose Option D: "No Improvement Required."
The proposal, though attractive at first glance, was found to be replete with loopholes which can have far-reaching consequences.

options.text: replete of loopholes which could have
replete with loopholes that could have
replete in loopholes that can have

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**replete with loopholes that could have**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The adjective **replete** identifies a state of being full or abundantly supplied. In the English language, it is a **linguistic fact** that **replete** must be followed by the **fixed preposition** **with** to form a grammatically correct **collocation**.
 
• The sentence utilizes the **past tense** verb **was found** in the principal clause. To maintain **tense consistency** (also known as the **sequence of tenses**), the subordinate clause describing the potential of the loopholes must use the past form of the modal verb. Therefore, **could** is required instead of **can**.
 
• The relative pronoun **that** is preferred here to introduce a **restrictive relative clause**. This clause is essential to the sentence as it defines the specific nature of the **loopholes** that made the proposal problematic.
 
• The phrase **could have** correctly expresses **past possibility** or potential, aligning with the observation made when the proposal was first evaluated.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• **Prepositional Usage:**
 
 
• **Replete of:** This is a **grammatical error** often caused by confusion with the phrase 'full of'. While they share meanings, their **syntactic requirements** differ.
 
• **Replete in:** This variation is generally restricted to **scientific** or **biological contexts**, such as a substance being 'replete in nutrients', and does not apply to abstract flaws like **loopholes**.
 
 
 
• **Modal Verb Logic:**
 
 
• The use of **can** in the original sentence creates a **tense mismatch**. In formal writing, if the discovery (**was found**) happened in the past, the potential consequences are viewed from that **past perspective**, necessitating **could**.
 
• **Could** also functions as a **subjunctive mood** marker here, indicating a hypothetical outcome based on the existing flaws in the **proposal**.
 
 
</ul

questions.solution:

**__Key Points__**

 
• The paragraph begins with a metaphor comparing a person's actions to those of a **philanthropist** whose **altruistic motives** unexpectedly lead to a **lucrative investment**.
 
• **Sentence D follows S1** as it directly continues the **philanthropist metaphor**, detailing the specific **ten percent reward** and the resulting **awkward feeling** that the profit detracts from the **savour of his virtue**.

• **Sentence B is the fifth sentence** as it expands on **Isabel Longstaffe’s** character, describing her **meticulous uprightness**, her **exacting code**, and her tendency to express **disapproval** through **cold silence**.
 
• The fixed sentence **S2 concludes the sequence** by emphasizing the finality of **Isabel's judgement**, which is a direct consequence of the **uprightness** described in sentence B.
 
• The correct sequence is **DACB**.

He was like the **philanthropist** who with **altruistic motives** builds model dwellings for the poor and finds that he has made a **lucrative investment**. She measured the standards of others by her own **meticulous uprightness** and there could be no greater **censure** than the **cold silence** with which she expressed her **disapproval** of a conduct that did not satisfy her **exacting code**. questions.question:
A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. If you feel Options A, B, or C do not improve the sentence, then choose Option D: "No improvement required."
His argument was not entirely wrong, but it overlooked several key points that would have made it more convincing.

options.text: His argument was not so wrong

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**No improvement required**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The original sentence **not entirely wrong** is grammatically sound and conveys a **nuanced meaning**, suggesting that the argument held **partial validity** or some degree of truth.
 
• The **adverb of degree** **entirely** correctly modifies the adjective **wrong**. When preceded by **not**, it indicates that the statement is **partially correct**, which fits the context of an argument that could be improved.
 
• The **adversative conjunction** **but** is used appropriately to introduce a **contrast** between the argument's **limited accuracy** and its **failure to include** essential details.
 
• The **conditional perfect construction** **would have made** in the second clause implies that the argument had a **persuasive foundation** that was simply **incomplete**, justifying the use of **not entirely wrong** in the first clause.
 
• Other options either change the **logical intent** of the sentence or introduce **less formal phrasing** that reduces the **analytical precision** of the statement.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• **Adverbs of Degree**:
 
 
• **Entirely**, **completely**, and **totally** are used to emphasize the **full extent** of a quality. In **formal writing**, negating these adverbs is a common **rhetorical strategy** to provide **tempered criticism**.
 
 
 
• **Logic and Coherence**:
 
 
• If an argument is **entirely wrong**, it usually requires **refutation** rather than just adding **key points** to make it **more convincing**. Therefore, the original phrasing maintains **logical coherence**.
 
 
 
• **Diction**:
 
 
• The phrase **not so wrong** is often considered **colloquial** or **idiomatic** and lacks the **formal weight** required for **argumentative prose** compared to **not entirely wrong**.
 
 
</ul
